stories.title: Swox Candidate Profile - Tanya Gillis
stories.summary: Tanya Gillis would like to help residents have their voices heard as the Ward 6 Councillor for South-West Oxford.
stories.author: Marcie Culbert
stories.content:
News Home

Wednesday, 26 August 2026 12:05

By Marcie Culbert X @marcieculbert

Tanya Gillis would like to help residents have their voices heard as the Ward 6 Councillor for South-West Oxford.

Swox - She wants to make a difference in her hometown community.

Tanya Gillis was born and raised in Beachville and she has decided to run for the Ward 6 councillor position in South-West Oxford.

"The mom hat is not needed as much as it used to be and I'd just love to help my community out and have their voices heard."

Gillis is a senior account technician for an accounting firm in Ingersoll and she has also been the President of the Beachville Parks and Rec Society for six years now. She has been involved in lots of other aspects of the community over the years, whether it's teaching Sunday school, helping with public school events, or dedicating her time to the local museum.

She is excited to see fibre internet coming to Beachville because it would benefit a lot of small businesses in the area.

If she's elected, she also wants to make sure all residents have their voices heard.

"I like to see diversity in a council, so being a woman I think that's important because South-West Oxford has only had one female representative in the last little bit and unfortunately she passed away. I think it's good to have a diversity of different ages and different genders so everybody is represented and has a voice."

The municipal election is scheduled for October 26th.

stories.title: Ilderton, Ont. vocal coach helps Rush’s Geddy Lee through ‘Fifty Something’ tour
stories.summary: He has one of the most recognizable voices in Canadian music. But after 11 years away from performing regularly, Geddy Lee, of Rush, had to rediscover that voice.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
He has one of the most recognizable voices in Canadian music. But after 11 years away from performing regularly, Geddy Lee, of Rush, had to rediscover that voice. “I found out, and it was a shock that I was his first vocal coach,” exclaimed Ilderton, Ont. based vocal coach Mitch Seekins.

“He never studied voice before. So, everything that he’s done has been completely natural up to that point, which is incredibly rare.” A vocal coach for more than 35 years, Seekins was contacted in spring 2025 to help Lee prepare for Rush’s Fifty Something Tour.

With Lee now in his 70s, Seekins knew the work would be demanding. “The Rush repertoire in my mind has got to be the most difficult rock gig to sing because it’s so high, and it stays so high, the whole show. He rarely gets a break.

So, does he have that in him anymore? What has the aging process done,” wondered the long-time voice expert. Seekins worked with Lee nearly every day for four months, helping to build his voice to withstand the rigors of touring.

The rock icon proved to be a highly disciplined student,” said Seekins. “And he started to see the progress starting to happen, and things were coming back. And it was a lot of work. But thank goodness he’s focused, very focused,” he explained.

While Geddy Lee is his most notable, a who’s who of great talents can be found among Seekins’ roster of students, including Luke Bentham of Canadian rock band, The Dirty Nil. “My imagination is kind of pushed to its limits kind of imagining what the rebuilding process would be like after taking such a sustained break as Geddy has.

And it makes it all the more impressive when I watch the footage of them playing this tour that they’re on,” Bentham said. Seekins has also taken on Rush guitarist Alex Lifeson as a student. Lifeson’s vocal role in Rush performances has historically been relatively minimal, but he wanted to expand his involvement for the current tour.

stories.title: Woodstock Police Briefs - Aug. 26th, 2026
stories.summary: Four incidents all result in drivers being charged with impaired operation of a vehicle.
stories.author: Kyle Freel
stories.content:
News Home

Wednesday, 26 August 2026 10:51

By Kyle Freel X @KFreelHeartFM

Four incidents all result in drivers being charged with impaired operation of a vehicle.

Woodstock - A transport truck driver is facing impaired driving charges.

The Woodstock Police were made aware of a transport truck stuck in a field last Friday at 2 a.m.

Officers found the truck stuck on an embankment near Oxford Road 4 and the driver inside. As a result, a 53-year-old Woodstock man is facing charges of operation while impaired by alcohol and drugs, along with operation while impaired with a blood alcohol concentration of 80 plus.

He was released on an undertaking.

Woodstock - The Woodstock Police have caught an impaired driver.

On Sunday at 2:45 a.m., officers received a report of a possible impaired driver in a parking lot in the area of Dundas Street. Officers located the vehicle, saw a woman get into the driver's seat, and conducted a traffic stop. During the investigation, an Approved Screening Device test was administered, resulting in an Alert.

As a result, a 34-year-old Port Loring woman was issued a seven-day driver's licence suspension.

Woodstock - A Woodstock man is in trouble with police in his home city.

Last Saturday at 3:45 p.m., Woodstock Police were on patrol and noticed a vehicle failing to stop at stop signs. Officers conducted a traffic stop, and the Approved Screening Device registered a fail.

As a result, the 79-year-old was arrested and charged with operation while impaired by alcohol and dangerous operation.

Woodstock - The Woodstock Police have stopped another impaired driver on city streets.

Around 11 p.m. last Saturday, officers noticed a vehicle going at speeds not consistent with the posted signs. There was a traffic stop was conducted, which resulted in the driver failing an Approved Screening Device test.

As a result, the 39-year-old Woodstock man is facing charges of operation while impaired by alcohol, operation while impaired with a blood alcohol concentration over 80, and possession of a schedule 1 substance - cocaine.

stories.title: Jerome Rancourt ready to lead Western Mustangs as starting QB
stories.summary: When 6-foot-5-inches Western Mustangs quarterback Jerome Rancourt rolls out of the pocket, it’s a nightmare for defensive backs.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
When 6-foot-5-inches Western Mustangs quarterback Jerome Rancourt rolls out of the pocket, it’s a nightmare for defensive backs. “It’s definitely not the corner’s first choice to tackle when he rolls out,” said Dasani McIntosh, Mustangs wide receiver.

The fifth-year quarterback from Quebec City, Que. is the new starter after Evan Hillock graduated. His transition from backup to starter comes at new head coach and quarterback guru Michael Faulds installs new schemes. “We have him as a head coach, but most of the time he’s our quarterback coach,” said Rancourt.

“We spent a lot of time including a couple of days before the camp started, we had a little retreat. All the quarterbacks went over the playbook threw some balls and it’s been very good.” Rancourt has been used in third-down and short-yardage situations over the past four seasons which has resulted in him racking up 25 rushing touchdowns.

His size has made him the perfect player in those scenarios. “I think everyone knows he’s a bruising runner,” said Faulds. “He can throw the ball a mile, but he’s really worked on his accuracy and his touch. I think it’s going to present some challenges for opposing defensive coordinators.

Is he going to take off with his legs? Is he going to drop back and throw it? He always has a stable of running backs behind him, led by the nation’s leading rusher Ethan Dolby last year.” For the receiver group like McIntosh, it opens up the passing game when a quarterback is a dual threat.

“Just more second chance plays,” said McIntosh. “Anytime the play breaks down, we know Jerome’s going to keep it alive. Guys like me with a little bit of speed; we’re definitely going to try to either take the top off or come back to the ball and try to make things happen.” He’s also seen Rancourt develop the mid-range passing game.

“When Jerome throws the ball, you have to be ready,” added McIntosh who had two receiving touchdowns in 2025. “He definitely has a ton of arm strength, but he’s just working on those intermediate throws. He could run the ball.

He could throw the deep ball. Just having a bit more touch is something that he’s added to his game in the summer.” In a season of change, Rancourt is set to take on the leadership role. He’s been grinding all offseason to handle the workload.

“I was also prepping for the CFL combine as a tight end, but I knew there was a possibility of me coming back,” said Rancourt. “Eventually I decided that was going to be the way. So, I was working with the guys a lot in the winter and then came back a couple of weeks earlier in the summer to make sure we were ready before camp.” One more week of work, then Western will open their season against York on Sept.

6. “Now it’s just about getting the boys ready,” said Rancourt.

stories.title: A 19-year-old woman killed in tractor trailer collision in Thunder Bay
stories.summary: OPP say officers and paramedics responded to the crash between a passenger vehicle and tractor-trailer at Mapleward Road and Highway 11-17 around 12:30 p.m. Tuesday.
stories.author: David Augustine
stories.content:
A 19-year-old woman has died following an afternoon car crash with a tractor-trailer in Thunder Bay, Ontario.

Ontario Provincial Police say officers and paramedics responded to the crash between a passenger vehicle and tractor-trailer at Mapleward Road and Highway 11-17 around 12:30 p.m. Tuesday.

Officers say the woman from Thunder Bay was taken to hospital, where she was pronounced dead.

Police have not released the woman’s name or provided details about what led to the collision.

A section of Highway 11-17 was closed for several hours for the investigation, but has since reopened.

Police are asking anyone who witnessed the crash or has dashcam footage from the area to contact them.

stories.title: 2 belugas, 4 dolphins from Marineland heading to aquarium in Spain
stories.summary: Marineland had originally sold all of its 30 belugas and four dolphins to an aquarium in China, but Ottawa blocked the move, saying it violated the spirit of a 2019 law.
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
Two belugas and four dolphins from Marineland are being moved today to an aquarium in Spain.

This is the fifth move of whales from the shuttered theme park in Niagara Falls, Ont., as it moves all of its animals off the property.

Marineland is up for sale and has said it is running out of money and can no longer afford to care for its animals.

The park had originally sold all of its 30 belugas and four dolphins to an aquarium in China, but the federal government blocked the move, saying it violated the spirit of a 2019 law.

That law banned whale and dolphin captivity, and forbade breeding and performances.

After today’s move to Oceanografic Valencia, there will be six belugas remaining in Marineland, which are soon set to head to an aquarium in the United States.

Echo, Lida, Marina and Tsunami are the dolphins leaving Canada, the last captive dolphins in the country. They will be joined en route by belugas Cleopatra and Jelly Bean.

The remaining belugas are the last captive whales in Canada.

After Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson nixed the move to China, Marineland threatened to euthanize all of its belugas and whales unless the federal government provided an emergency infusion of cash.

The park then turned to a consortium of American and Spanish aquariums for help.

The world’s largest collective move of captive whales has so far seen belugas shipped to SeaWorld locations in San Diego and San Antonio, the Shedd Aquarium in Chicago and the Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta.

stories.title: Booming Toronto-based burger joint Rudy expands into London, St. Thomas
stories.summary: "What we aim for is a very simple menu, simple food done right, and that's what we do."
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
Rudy, a Toronto-based burger shop that opened in 2016, has been steadily expanding into Southwestern Ontario this year, with a restaurant at London’s White Oaks Mall and another set to open in St. Thomas on Sept. 11 at 985 Talbot St. Luke McCann, owner of the growing chain, spoke with Lfp’s Ryan Goodison on their recipe for success.

Q: For those who might not know you, what is Rudy and how did it start?

A: A buddy of mine and I started it over 10 years ago in Little Italy on College Street in Toronto, and it was a very simple concept. We were both burger fans growing up, and did a lot of travelling trying to figure out what we wanted to do. But the idea was basically just a simple griddle burger. I remember my mom making them in the frying pan when I was a kid, and then the idea was to keep the menu very simple. It’s a scratch kitchen, so everything is made in house.

Q: Where does the name come from?

A: Rudy comes from when my former late business partner and I were kids. You go to a party or something like that, and somebody’s acting a little out of hand or obnoxious or a little full of themselves. We would quietly say that guy’s being a “rudy,” he’s being rude. It’s sort of just an inside joke that we had when were kids.

Q: You’re now expanding into St. Thomas, what made it the next step for you?

A: We went down and we looked around, we spoke to a lot of places, businesses in the area, and they all seemed to be doing really well, and it was a growing area of the province. We found an amazing location on Talbot with great signage, and it’s a standalone. It reminded US of our place on the Queensway in Toronto. So when you find a special location like that, it’s hard to pass up.

Q: You recently expanded into London in January, what made the city the right place for you?

New cafe brings taste of family's Colombia coffee farm to downtown London

Make it 70 years (and counting) for landmark London diner

A: London is a big city outside of Toronto and when you head in that direction you can see it’s growing. You’ve got colleges, universities, and it’s a big population, so we figured it just made sense. I’ve also got some friends that lived down there that would always message and say “Hey, when are you going to open up in London?” It had been on the radar for a while.

Q: Why was the location at White Oaks Mall the right fit?

A: We just sort of liked that area. It’s right off the highway, and I think the mall is under construction right now as well as the road construction. We feel that once all that’s done, it’s going to be booming. You have the Ronaldo soccer Footlab and the Ikea going into the same mall, so it just seemed like a good fit for US.

Q: The St. Thomas location will be your 19th across the province, what do you think is behind the success so far?

A: What we aim for is a very simple menu, simple food done right, and that’s what we do. We’re not as fast as McDonald’s, but we think it’s worth it. I think what really has helped US expand is attracting the right people to come work with US. If you have great people, you can do great things.

Q: Are you planning any further expansions into Southwestern Ontario?

A: This is a far southwest as we have on the books right now, but we’d like to get eventually to Windsor, and maybe Sarnia.

Q: If you could recommend one thing on the menu, what would it be?

A: My go-to is the double cheeseburger, which is called the Rude Dude. I usually get a side of our thin fries that we cook in beef tallow, and that’s another thing we do a little different from most places, although it is becoming more popular again.

A: What we aim for is a very simple menu, simple food done right, and that’s what we do. We’re not as fast as McDonald’s, but we think it’s worth it. I think what really has helped US expand is attracting the right people to come work with US. If you have great people, you can do great things.

content_blocks.text: Rudy, a Toronto-based burger shop that opened in 2016, has been steadily expanding into Southwestern Ontario this year, with a restaurant at London’s White Oaks Mall and another set to open in St. Thomas on Sept. 11 at 985 Talbot St. Luke McCann, owner of the growing chain, spoke with Lfp’s Ryan Goodison on their recipe for success.
Q: For those who might not know you, what is Rudy and how did it start?

A: A buddy of mine and I started it over 10 years ago in Little Italy on College Street in Toronto, and it was a very simple concept. We were both burger fans growing up, and did a lot of travelling trying to figure out what we wanted to do. But the idea was basically just a simple griddle burger. I remember my mom making them in the frying pan when I was a kid, and then the idea was to keep the menu very simple. It’s a scratch kitchen, so everything is made in house.
Q: Where does the name come from?

A: Rudy comes from when my former late business partner and I were kids. You go to a party or something like that, and somebody’s acting a little out of hand or obnoxious or a little full of themselves. We would quietly say that guy’s being a “rudy,” he’s being rude. It’s sort of just an inside joke that we had when were kids.

A: We went down and we looked around, we spoke to a lot of places, businesses in the area, and they all seemed to be doing really well, and it was a growing area of the province. We found an amazing location on Talbot with great signage, and it’s a standalone. It reminded US of our place on the Queensway in Toronto. So when you find a special location like that, it’s hard to pass up.
Q: You recently expanded into London in January, what made the city the right place for you?

stories.summary: The potato drive will support the Food Rescue Hub this Saturday.
stories.author: Marcie Culbert
stories.content:
News Home

Wednesday, 26 August 2026 07:20

By Marcie Culbert X @marcieculbert

The potato drive will support the Food Rescue Hub this Saturday.

Woodstock - The Great Potato Giveback is back for another year in the Friendly City.

It will be taking place at the Woodstock Zehrs this Saturday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m..

Chris Bracey says they will be selling 10lb bags of potatoes for $2.

"If people want to drop in, they will be able to buy a bag of potatoes right outside if they don't want to come into the store, and the customer can choose to buy it and keep it or buy it and donate it. Every bag that we sell that day, we're also going to donate $1."

Katlyn Mechanical will also donate an additional $1 for each bag, up to $2,000.

The event will also include a Lions Club barbeque, fun kids, games, and a potato soup contest.

The Woodstock Zehrs sold over 2,100 potatoes during the Great Potato Giveback last year, and over 800 potatoes were donated to Operating Sharing.

This year's event will support the Food Rescue Hub. Allison Henkell is one of the board members for the hub, and she says it will store food for agencies in need.

"There will be freezers, fridges and storage so we can take large amounts of food and various organizations can get just what they need, so we don't have large amounts of waste from there either."

The hub will be located on Winniett Street and if all goes as planned in terms of renovations, Henkel says the hub could open at the end of September. Volunteers will be needed once it opens, those who are interested can e-mail info@foodrescuehub.CA for more information.

Chris Bracey and Allison Henkell stopped by the Heart FM studio to chat with Liz and Marcie on Monday, August 24th. You can listen to the full interview below:

By Kyle Freel X @KFreelHeartFM

Swph is shining a light on overdoses ahead of International Overdose Awareness Day on August 31st.

Oxford County - Southwestern Public Health (Swph) is raising awareness on overdoses.

Partnering with the Oxford Mental Health and Addictions Action Coalition, there will be events taking place to raise awareness, connect residents with supports and resources, and honour lives lost to overdose. The first event happened yesterday afternoon in Museum Square, while today the booth will be set up at Operation Sharing from 11:00 a.m. until 2:00 p.m. The final event will be tomorrow outside Tillsonburg Mall from 10:00 a.m. until noon.

Anyone that comes to an event will have access to naloxone training, information about local programs and services, opportunities to connect with community partners, and space to honour those who have died from overdose.

If you are not able to attend one of the events in Oxford County, but want to participate you can do so by going online to the International Overdose Awareness Day website .

stories.author: Marcie Culbert
stories.content:
News Home

Wednesday, 26 August 2026 06:59

By Marcie Culbert X @marcieculbert

Parton was a musician, actress, businesswoman and philanthropist.

Nashville - After a brief battle with cancer, Dolly Parton has passed away at the age of 80.

Her nephew, Bryan Seaver, shared the news in a video posted Parton's social media pages yesterday.

Parton was an iconic country music artist with several hit songs including Jolene , 9 to 5 , and I Will Always Love You .

Her film credits included Steel Magnolias , Joyful Noise , and Dolly Parton's Coat of Many Colors . She also made several appearances in TV shows over the years including Reba , Hannah Montana , The Simpsons , and The Magic School Bus .

Parton was also a philanthropist and successful businesswoman with the Dollywood theme park in Smoky Mountain foothills and her education non-profit, Imagination Library, that send free books to children.

stories.title: Ottawa Reveals Retaliatory Tariffs for US Products
stories.summary: Retaliatory tariffs for nearly 900 American products will take effect on September 8th.
stories.author: Marcie Culbert
stories.content:
News Home

Wednesday, 26 August 2026 06:23

By Marcie Culbert X @marcieculbert

Retaliatory tariffs for nearly 900 American products will take effect on September 8th.

Ottawa - Ottawa has released more details about the retalitory tariffs against the United States.

They will affect nearly 900 American products starting September 8th.

Officials say American steel and aluminum tariffs will be doubled to 50 percent. There will also 50 percent tariffs for smartphones, golf clubs, gaming consoles, fishing rods, clothing, furniture, perfumes and more.

There will be a 25 percent tariff on appliances, agricultural machinery, dairy products, seafood and certain steel and aluminum derivatives products. A 15 percent tariff will also affect a small list of items including hand tools, air conditioners, forklifts, and more.

Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne stating the following during the announcement yesterday.

"When the United States of America asked too much and offered too little, we made a choice. We chose Canada."

This is in response to the 50 percent tariffs the United States announced for $28 billion worth of Canadian goods last week.

Ottawa also announced $7.5 billion support package for business affected by the US tariffs yesterday.

stories.title: Council nixes homeless shelter guideline about illegal drug possession—leaving status quo or confusion?
stories.summary: London won’t enact a new drug policy for taxpayer-funded emergency homeless shelters meant to clarify and standardize admission rules, but the decision faced sharp criticism for being politically motivated and confusing.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
London won’t enact a new drug policy for taxpayer-funded emergency homeless shelters meant to clarify and standardize admission rules, but the decision faced sharp criticism for being politically motivated and confusing.

The 2026 Emergency Shelter Guidelines aim to modernize the 15 year old policy , including a clause that possessing illegal drugs should not automatically prevent someone from entering a shelter However on Tuesday, Council voted 9-6 in support of an amendment by Coun.

Susan Stevenson to “remove any provision that permits illegal substances to be brought into or possessed within emergency shelter locations.” “There’s a strawman argument put out there, oh, who’s going to strip search them to make sure there’s nothing in there?” Stevenson asserted.

“It’s a far cry from saying that, and that (drugs) are allowed.” Stevenson argued that the change doesn’t block admission, it simply leaves the updated guidelines silent on the issue of drug possession inside emergency shelters.

“Now we’re making a decision that’s going to create confusion, and this is not an area where we need to be confused,” countered Coun. David Ferreira. Deputy Mayor Shawn Lewis suggested omitting the clause would create the potential for a drug-free shelter in the future for homeless Londoners without active addictions.

“It’s just simply going to be up to the shelter providers,” explained Lewis. “If someone chooses to come forward through the [procurement)]process and offer a space that is [drug] possession free, then that will be their choice.” “I think what this is doing is it’s muddying the waters, and we’re returning to a place of ambiguity,” responded Coun.

Hadleigh McAlister. McAlister then suggested a motivation behind the motion. “I don’t like how it has been used for political posturing purposes,” he told colleagues. “We’re not debating a war on drugs here. This is not a pro and anti-drug vote.” City staff emphasized that denying entry to a shelter because someone has a medical condition, including addiction, would potentially be grounds for a Human Rights complaint.

Initially the change was defeated 7-8, but Lewis immediately notified colleagues that he accidentally voted incorrectly. A second vote flipped the result, removing of the clause regarding illegal drug possession. After the meeting, Mayor Josh Morgan reiterated that the decision lets shelters maintain their current rules, “The [shelter] providers can continue as they would.

They can follow all applicable laws. There’s some legislation in the Human Rights area about addictions being a disability, and you can’t deny service. The onus there would be on the shelters to continue to follow those laws and guidelines.”

stories.title: One more chance for thunderstorms before sun-filled weekend
stories.summary: We’ll see a mix of sun and cloud Wednesday with temperatures climbing this afternoon.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
We’ll see a mix of sun and cloud Wednesday with temperatures climbing this afternoon. The high reaching 26 degrees, feeling like 31. “We have a chance for rain coming in tonight in advance of a cold front with the possibility of a thunderstorm Thursday,” explained CTV London Meteorologist Julie Atchison.

Conditions clear up by Friday with mainly sunny skies expected. “The weekend is shaping up to be a good one. Sunshine to a mix of sun and cloud. We could use a dry weekend in southern Ontario with daytime highs coming towards the mid 20s,” said Atchison.

Here’s a look at the rest of the forecast Wednesday: A mix of sun and cloud. Becoming sunny in the afternoon. Fog patches dissipating early in the morning. Wind becoming south 30 km/h in the morning. High 26. Humidex 31.

UV index 7 or high. Wednesday night: Becoming cloudy in the evening with 60 per cent chance of showers late in the evening and overnight. Risk of a thunderstorm late in the evening and after midnight. Wind south 20 km/h becoming light in the evening.

Wind becoming southwest 20 gusting to 40 near midnight. Low 18. Thursday: A mix of sun and cloud with 40 per cent chance of showers. High 24. Friday: Sunny. High 23. Saturday: Sunny. High 25. Sunday: A mix of sun and cloud.

stories.title: What’s in a name? Trump’s ‘Lake America’ threat raises questions about centuries of history
stories.summary: Donald Trump is threatening to rename Lake Ontario, but a Great Lakes historian says the name carries centuries of Indigenous and regional history.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Touria Izri
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump is threatening to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America,” but the name has centuries of history behind it.

Trump said Tuesday the United States is giving “serious consideration” to changing the name of Lake Ontario as relations with Canada, and particularly Ontario, sour amid an escalating trade dispute.

He later posted a graphic depicting the Great Lake under the proposed “Lake America” name.

The threat came a day after Trump and Ontario Premier Doug Ford publicly traded insults as tensions over the Canada-U.S. trade dispute escalated.

Ford dismissed the proposed name change during an interview with CNN on Tuesday. “I think it’s a lot of rhetoric,” Ford told Cnn’s Wolf Blitzer.

For Mary Baxter, a PhD candidate in Western University’s history department who specializes in Great Lakes environmental history, the threat immediately brought to mind the Republican president’s executive order last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico.

“My first reaction was to think of the whole Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America incident,” Baxter told Global News.

“There are times when we’ve heard Trump back down, but there are also times where he moved ahead with things. And this is one of those things that he could move ahead on,” she said.

Trump signed an executive order last year directing the U.S. government to use the name Gulf of America. But Lake Ontario’s name has a much longer history than either Canada or the United States.

Baxter said the name Ontario comes from an Iroquoian language term and roughly translates to “sparkling waters.”

The lake has been known by several names over its history, including different names used by First Nations before European contact.

Baxter said French explorers also used different names for the lake, while the French and British had competing names for it during their conflicts in North America.

The French often referred to it as Lac Frontenac, she said, while the British at times used Cataraqui Lake, another name with Iroquoian origins.

By the mid-1700s — before the American Revolution and the eventual creation of Canada and the United States — Lake Ontario had emerged as the name that stuck.

The first known appearance of “Lake Ontario” on a map dates to 1656, Baxter said, and the name has been used intermittently ever since.

Baxter said the name was appearing on maps more than a century before the United States declared independence and long before there was a province called Ontario.

“I think that there can sometimes be a perception out there that the Great Lakes have been named after the communities that surround them,” Baxter said.

But she said the opposite is true.

“These communities got their names from the lakes. These names are older.”

Ontario, the province, was named for the lake, and not the other way around.

Lake Ontario is one of five Great Lakes and straddles the Canada-U.S. border, with Ontario to its north and New York state to its south. The Great Lakes — Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie and Superior — are a chain of five freshwater lakes that hold roughly one-fifth of the world’s surface fresh water.

Daniel Macfarlane, an environmental historian at Western Michigan University and author of The Lives of Lake Ontario , told Global the lake occupies a much more central place in Canada’s history and identity than it does in the United States.

“It’s far more important to Canada than it is also to the United States,” Macfarlane said. He described Lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence River as forming the heart of early Canada.

“We’ve got like a quarter of the Canadian population living near Lake Ontario, which far outnumbers the New York side,” Macfarlane said.

Canada and the United States do not necessarily have to use the same name for a geographic feature they share, Baxter said, pointing to international examples in which countries use different names for the same body of water, such as the Sea of Japan, which South Korea refers to as the East Sea.

That means a U.S. decision to adopt “Lake America” would not necessarily require Canada to follow suit.

Baxter said disputes over geographic names are not unusual, but they frequently emerge within broader political conflicts. “There is a lot of global history of that happening, but it frequently happens during conflicts, which is what we have here,” she said. “So it reflects significance.”

In this case, Baxter said the history embedded in the Great Lakes’ names makes the question more complicated. “There is an Indigenous heritage that is embedded in some of these lakes’ names. So when you change that name, there’s a rewriting of a very long history,” she said.

She said changing the name could be seen as dishonouring Indigenous communities that have lived along the lake for centuries and continue to make its shores their home.

Baxter said those communities should have a central voice in any discussion about changing the lake’s name.

There could also be business consequences if the United States goes ahead with a name change. Baxter pointed to businesses and organizations that have incorporated Lake Ontario into their names and could be forced to decide whether to adapt if the U.S. government began officially referring to it as Lake America.

“There’s a bureaucratic process that goes into that,” she said, describing the potential consequences as “a lot of make-busy work.”

Trump’s comments come as Canada and the U.S. are locked in a worsening trade dispute .

Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended trade talks Friday, accusing the United States of introducing last-minute demands that would limit Canada’s ability to make trade agreements with other countries and protect its culture and sovereignty.

The United States imposed a new round of 50 per cent tariffs on $28 billion worth of Canadian exports Saturday, while Canada announced retaliatory measures Tuesday that are set to take effect Sept. 8.

–With files from Aaron D’Andrea, Isaac Callan and Colin D’Mello

stories.title: Former Iranian official living in Toronto was ‘critical’ to terror finance, Cbsa alleges
stories.summary: A Cbsa report alleges that as a deputy director in Iran’s Ministry of Industry, Mines and Trade, Abbas Omidi, assisted the regime's state sponsorship of terrorism.
stories.author: Stewart Bell
stories.content:
A former Iranian official now living in Toronto had a “critical” role in helping the Islamic Republic generate revenue needed to fund Middle East terror groups, according to government documents obtained by Global News.

A Canada Border Services Agency report released on Tuesday alleges that as a deputy director in Iran’s Ministry of Industry, Mines and Trade, Abbas Omidi , assisted with the regime’s state sponsorship of terrorism.

The 2024 report, which details why Omidi should be expelled from Canada, said the Iranian mining sector in which he served at a senior level was closely linked to the military and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

“As a result of his power and influence, the subject directly benefited the Iranian economy and the government’s ability to continue to fund terrorism and human rights abuses throughout the world,” the Cbsa wrote.

“As the only individual qualified to continue to perform his specific role, the subject was critical in the Iranian government’s continued ability to draw in mining revenue and fund the military, weapons manufacturing, and terrorism, both foreign and domestic.”

The report was among hundreds of pages of documents disclosed to the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) at Omidi’s deportaton hearing earlier this year. The IRB released a redacted version at the request of Global News.

The Cbsa is trying to deport Omidi on the grounds he was a longtime senior official in Iran’s repressive regime. The refugee board said Wednesday the hearing was concluded and its decision on the case was expected in the fall.

Before arriving in Canada as a visitor in 2022, Omidi was an official in Iran’s mining and trade ministry. The Cbsa alleged in its report that he “exerted significant influence on the exercise of government power.”

He is among 37 suspected senior Iranian regime members found living in Canada since the government launched a crackdown against them in 2022 in response to Tehran’s suppression of protests.

Omidi’s deportation hearing began in March. Although he tried to ban the press from the proceedings, Global News successfully fought his application for a private hearing.

The allegations that Omidi helped Iran’s regime make the money it needed to support terrorist groups did not come up at his hearing, but the Cbsa report on him repeatedly mentions the issue.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (Irgc) relies “heavily” on mining revenues to support regional terror groups, the Cbsa said in its report on the 56-year-old Iranian citizen.

“The abundant amount of wealth generated from the mining industry allows the Iranian regime and specifically, the Irgc, to continue to be a state sponsor of terrorism,” the report said.

“The Irgc has consistently provided financial and other material support including financing, training, technology transfer, advanced weapons, guidance, or direction to a broad range of terrorist organizations.”

They include Lebanon’s Hezbollah as well as Kata’ib Hizballah, a Shia Iraqi militia that has allegedly claimed responsibility for attacks in Europe and shootings targeting the U.S. consulate and a synagogue in Toronto.

The Irgc provides up to $100 million to Palestinian terror groups Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, the report said.

Its support for Hezbollah totals $700 million, while another $300 million is allotted to other terror factions, according to the Cbsa.

“Considering that the mining sector is responsible for approximately 40 percent of Iran’s gross domestic product, the regime’s ability to fund the Irgc, army, and foreign terrorist organizations is heavily dependent on the success of the mining industry,” the Cbsa said.

Omidi “directly and significantly impacted and benefited the Iranian economy and the government’s ability to continue to fund its military, weapons production, and terrorism and human rights abuses throughout the world,” the report said.

It added that he did so while earning a salary “four times higher than the national average.”

Omidi’s lawyer did not respond to requests for comment.

At his hearing, Omidi acknowledged he had served as a deputy director general in the ministry of mining but downplayed his importance, insisting his role was mostly technical.

Iranian Canadians have long complained that past and present members of the brutal regime they fled were turning up in the country and treating it as a safe haven.

The federal government banned all senior officials of the Iranian government from Canada four years ago, but has struggled to deport them.

According to figures released by the Cbsa on Aug. 4, immigration enforcement officers have launched 182 investigations into suspected “senior officials of the Iranian regime” in Canada.

Eight of them left Canada before their deportations hearings began. The IRB has issued deportation orders against four more on the grounds they were top regime members.

Two have been removed. The Cbsa confirmed to Global News on Aug. 17 that the latest to go was Syed Salman Samani , who was Iran’s deputy interior minister.

The Cbsa said it was in the process of expelling two more, which would bring the total number who have left Canada to 12.

Fifty-two investigations are still underway, according to the department’s figures.

Separately, the Cbsa has launched deportation proceedings against 51 Iranian citizens based on their membership in the Irgc , a listed terrorist entity under Canadian law.

“Final decisions on these allegations are made by the IRB after an admissibility hearing. In nine of these cases, the alleged Irgc member departed Canada prior to an admissibility hearing,” the Cbsa said.

Stewart.Bell@globalnews.CA

stories.summary: Isn’t it sad our mayor is going to be rewarded for a 28 per cent tax increase during three years? There does not appear to be any serious contender for the position.
stories.author: Free Press Readers
stories.content:
Isn’t it sad our mayor is going to be rewarded for a 28 per cent tax increase during three years? There does not appear to be any serious contender for the position.

Working in business for many years, I have never seen a person submit a budget request like the police department did and get everything they wanted. We need someone to stand up for the taxpayer and challenge budgets like it was their own money.

Maybe in another four years people will see the light.

Gary Rogers, London

I can’t think of a more important issue facing Londoners at this time, so let’s demand that candidates address it.

Dogs frequently ingest corn cobs whole or in pieces, resulting in a bowel obstruction. Please, keep corn cobs out of reach.

Paul Francis, Thorndale

stories.title: Victoria Park enhancements to brighten visitor experience year-round
stories.summary: Victoria Park is set to become even more welcoming with upgraded lighting and accessible viewing features, enhancing community e
stories.content:
Victoria Park is set to become even more welcoming with upgraded lighting and accessible viewing features , enhancing community events and everyday park use throughout the year. Improvements include new multi-colored LED lighting surrounding the concrete pad and the interior of the bandshell, along with a portable raised seating area that will feature railings and a wheelchair-accessible ramp.

The improvements are made possible through a $165,000 donation from Canada Life, recognizing the company's deep roots in London as it celebrates 100 years at its downtown location. Coinciding with the City's Bicentennial, the investment will enhance one of London's most cherished public spaces while improving accessibility and the visitor experience.

The upgraded lighting will help create a more vibrant atmosphere for festivals, community gatherings and public skating, while the new accessible viewing area will allow more Londoners to comfortably experience performances and events.

"Victoria Park has been bringing Londoners together for generations, and these improvements will ensure even more people can enjoy everything this important community space has to offer," says Cheryl Smith, Deputy City Manager, Neighbourhood and Community-Wide Services. "We're grateful for Canada Life's generous donation, which will create a vibrant and accessible destination for residents and visitors alike."

"Having spent nearly 40 years working in downtown London, I know firsthand how Victoria Park has long been at the heart of community life in London, bringing people together to celebrate, connect and create lasting memories," says Jeff Van Hoeve, Senior Vice-President, Business Integration, Canada Life. “As Canada Life marks 100 years in downtown London, we're proud to support improvements that will help make this treasured public space more accessible and enjoyable for residents and visitors for years to come."

The improvements support Victoria Park's role as one of London's premier gathering spaces, creating a more accessible and welcoming destination for residents and visitors for years to come.

stories.title: Trading the news desk for the yoga mat
stories.summary: Reform Pilates Studio in Grand Bend Ont. has grown in popularity since social media transformed the workout into a global trend.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
Reform Pilates Studio in Grand Bend Ont. has grown in popularity since social media transformed the workout into a global trend. Britt Britton, founder of Reform Pilates Studio, said she recognizes the role social media plays in her business.

“Pilates has blown up over social media and the industry itself has really been thriving with that blow up,” said Britton. “I find with Reform in particular, it’s been such a great platform to showcase Pilates, it can be challenging but also really really fun.” Britton said one of the biggest misconceptions she’s noticed on social media is that Pilates is easy.

“It looks easy,” said Britton. “We like to use the word humbling.”

stories.title: Uncertainty about temporary winter homeless shelter’s location sparks debate about clustering in core business districts
stories.summary: City Council has supported the latest version of London’s Winter Response to Homelessness, but tensions resurfaced during the debate about the location of a temporary shelter that will be operated by Ark Aid Street Mission.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
City council has supported the latest version of London’s Winter Response to Homelessness, but tensions resurfaced during the debate about the location of a temporary shelter that will be operated by Ark Aid Street Mission.

The updated plan will see homeless shelters open a total of 235 overnight spaces every night between Dec. 1, 2026, and March 31, 2027, plus an additional 29 overnight spaces when temperatures drop below -15C or -20 windchill.

Most of the spaces will be within existing shelters, but Ark Aid Street Mission is looking to secure a yet-to-be-determined location for 40 spaces that would operate nightly from 9 p.m. to 9 a.m. Concerned about the clustering of frontline agencies in the Old East Village (OEV) BIA, Coun.

Susan Stevenson proposed requiring council approval of the location before it receives municipal funding. “To say that there are no other locations [but the main street of core area BIAs] is counter to our whole objective of 12 to 15 [homeless] hubs around the city,” she asserted.

Coun. Hadleigh McAlister expressed similar concern about the Hamilton Road BIA in his ward, “We need to recognize that we have repeatedly asked two areas of the city to shoulder the responsibility and that is grossly unfair.” Downtown London Coun.

David Ferreira acknowledged, “I understand the capacity that we have is really within these [core] areas, however, I also see that there is a reality that we do have service providers within a small area.” Stevenson pressed staff about a previous council decision not to fund shelter spaces on the main streets of BIAs, but council supported a “not withstanding” amendment essentially exempting this decision from the previous restriction.

Deputy Mayor Shawn Lewis rejected the notion that council continues to cluster frontline services for homeless Londoners in OEV, Downtown London, and along Hamilton Road. “The core is not the only location where we have homelessness services,” Lewis stated.

“On Clarke Road in the east end I have the YOU (Youth Opportunities Unlimited) youth shelter. I also have the Anova Women’s Shelter. South of [Highway] 401 is where we put the micro-modular shelter.” The deputy mayor emphasized that The Ark and Unity Project own their buildings on Dundas Street in the OEV BIA and receive private donations to fund some of their operations.

“So if you want to talk about moving them, then you better talk about a multi-year budget business plan for property acquisition, to then do land swaps with them, because that is what you’re talking about,” he added.

stories.title: Drug-possession clause pulled from shelter guidelines after heated debate
stories.summary: Councillors traded accusations of “political posturing” as they split over how shelters should handle drug possession.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
Councillors traded accusations of “political posturing” as they split over how shelters should handle drug possession.

Accusations of political posturing, speculation and projection were among the barbs traded by city politicians as they made last-minute changes to guidelines for London’s homeless shelters.

City hall has been updating its emergency shelter guidelines for the first time since 2011, but a clause barring providers from disqualifying a potential resident based on possession of drugs proved controversial for a majority of council.

Led by Ward 4 Coun. Susan Stevenson, council voted 9-6 Tuesday to remove mention of that clause – leaving city hall silent on the issue of drug possession in shelters.

“How about we just not say that they’re allowed to bring in illegal substances, we’ll let staff work that out . . . without this council endorsing guidelines that allow illegal substances,” she said.

“We heard what the agencies said, we understand the concerns – there’s always a straw man argument out there like ‘Oh who’s going to strip search them to make sure that there’s nothing in there,’ there’s a far cry between that, and saying they’re allowed.”

Councillors Anna Hopkins, David Ferreira, Elizabeth Peloza, Skylar Franke, Sam Trosow and Hadleigh McAlister voted against the change, while all others voted in favour.

Politicians initially voted down removal of the clause 8-7, but deputy mayor Shawn Lewis called for reconsideration after voting incorrectly.

City hall sought to update the guidelines from the previous abstinence-based model to better reflect what shelter providers are currently facing. While residents would not be denied entry for drug possession, they would still be barred from using drugs inside the shelter.

Unity Project executive director Chuck Lazenby previously told politicians the abstinence policy led to people hiding their drugs and staff spending more time surveilling people than helping them, adding that hiding drugs amid today’s toxic supply was “a life and death issue.”

First 20 micro shelters for the homeless installed at London site

Overdose suspected in death at London micro-shelter: Site lead

The change prompted confusion among councillors about what removing the clause would actually mean. While city staff were unable to provide a definitive answer given the sudden reversal, deputy city manager of social and health development Kevin Dickins predicted confusion among service providers.

McAlister, the Ward 1 representative, said council was “muddying the waters” and argued the change effectively nullifies the substance of the updated guidelines.

“It’s not going to result in what people want unfortunately, I think you’re still going to see (drug addicted people) on the street,” he said.

“We all care about this issue, we’re all struggling with it, but I don’t like how it has been used for political posturing purposes – we’re not debating the war on drugs here . . . this is more US trying to have guidelines that allow operators to work in a difficult space.”

A motion to refer the guidelines back to committee to learn more about the implications was voted down.

Trosow referenced staff’s repeated assurances that problematic shelter residents could still be removed for behavioural issues and expressed concerns about possible human rights challenges.

“We’re going to be pushing people away who are in the most need,” he said. “We’re allowing posturing and political considerations to affect our judgment here, and that is not something that is acceptable, I find it reprehensible.”

Politicians in support of the change argued that drug possession is not being banned. Instead, with city hall silent on the issue, service providers would be left to establish their own standards.

Lewis said it would be “highly speculative” to say people would be turned away by shelter providers because of the change, while Mayor Josh Morgan said his colleagues were “projecting a whole lot on to the one change we made.”

“Removing references from the guideline does not change the way that the shelter operators can operate today,” Morgan said. “Being silent on something doesn’t preclude you from having to follow the rules of the provincial and federal governments and the human rights commission.”

Politicians also approved the 2026-27 winter homelessness response Tuesday, including new provisions for additional fire and bylaw compliance inspections.

The response calls for 235 beds and warming spaces to remain open from December through the end of March, with an additional 29 surge spaces when the temperature drops to -15 C or -20 C with the wind chill. The projected cost is $5.7 million, with $3.6 million already set aside from city reserves and the remainder covered by federal funding.

One proposed location includes 30 resting spaces at Ark Aid Street Mission’s Dundas Street building, where council voted 14-1 Tuesday in favour of a carve-out from the bylaw preventing city-funded overnight resting spaces on the main street of a business district . Stevenson was the sole opposing vote.

Politicians also approved the 2026-27 winter homelessness response Tuesday, including new provisions for additional fire and bylaw compliance inspections.

The response calls for 235 beds and warming spaces to remain open from December through the end of March, with an additional 29 surge spaces when the temperature drops to -15 C or -20 C with the wind chill. The projected cost is $5.7 million, with $3.6 million already set aside from city reserves and the remainder covered by federal funding.

One proposed location includes 30 resting spaces at Ark Aid Street Mission’s Dundas Street building, where council voted 14-1 Tuesday in favour of a carve-out from the bylaw preventing city-funded overnight resting spaces on the main street of a business district . Stevenson was the sole opposing vote.

stories.title: Ontario government takes next step towards possible nuclear plant on America’s doorstep
stories.summary: The Ontario government has taken the next step towards a potential nuclear power plant south of Sarnia, Ont., that could bring thousands of permanent and construction jobs.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
The Ontario government has taken the next step towards a potential nuclear power plant south of Sarnia, Ont., that could bring thousands of permanent and construction jobs. The announcement coincides with the ongoing war of words between Premier Doug Ford and U.S.

President Donald Trump. “You know, we’re up against a very real threat in this country,” said Ontario’s Minister of Energy and Mines, Stephen Lecce, while standing on the shoreline of St. Clair River, directly across from the U.S.

“We don’t need to be dependent on America, and energy security is important.” Lecce later announced the Ford government has committed to providing $500,000 to St. Clair Township. The money is earmarked to pay for consultations needed before any planning begins to put shovels in the ground.

He said discussions will include First Nations leaders. Until 2013, St. Clair Township was home to the coal-fired Lambton Generation Station. When it closed and was later demolished, more than 400 jobs and $2 million in tax revenue disappeared.

Now, there is far more on the table, although it remains ‘just talk’ for now, according to Mayor Jeff Agar. “I would have liked to have seen it go up four years ago, but it’s a process, right?” said Agar. While a nuclear option is the preference of the government, Lecce has conceded a natural gas plant is among options.

The mayor has made his choice. “Nuclear is the way to go,” he said. In response to a question from CTV News, the minister conceded President Trump’s comments have accelerated planning. “We are motivated to move fast and get this project done.” While a natural gas facility could be built within a few years, Lecce conceded a nuclear facility could take up to a decade.

But the payoff — he insisted — would be worth it. “This is jobs for our grandkids!” he concluded.

stories.title: Trade war escalation: New U.S. tariffs spark economic fears, could hit London SMEs hard
stories.summary: Escalating trade tensions with the U.S. have landed a significant blow to the London region’s economy, with new, steep tariffs threatening to disproportionately impact the city’s numerous small and medium-sized businesses.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
Escalating trade tensions with the U.S. have landed a significant blow to the London region’s economy, with new, steep tariffs threatening to disproportionately impact the city’s numerous small and medium-sized businesses (SMEs).

The recent tit-for-tat tariff announcements are adding considerable pressure to an economy already grappling with one of Canada’s highest unemployment rates for large urban centres. New U.S. tariffs, reportedly at 50 per cent on nearly $20 billion worth of Canadian exports, were announced Saturday, targeting a selective list of products that include key sectors for London.

Graham Henderson, CEO of the London Chamber of Commerce, warned that this isn’t just an issue for large manufacturers. “This isn’t a problem that is just facing big car manufacturers and steel manufacturers,” Henderson stated.

“This is an issue that’s going to impact probably disproportionately small and medium sized businesses, of which there are 14,000, I think, in London.” The impact is already being felt by local companies. For businesses like Vaughn Hockey, which manufactures specialized goalie equipment including now-tariffed sticks, or Black Fly Beverages, a local producer of alcoholic drinks, the tariffs present immediate challenges.

“If you’re making alcoholic beverages here in London and your market is in the U.S., you’re going to wake up with a 50 per cent headache,” Henderson explained. “And if your business model is based around selling into the U.S., that’s a problem.” The Chamber of Commerce’s own Op-Ed further illustrated this, noting that a 50 per cent tariff can make a product dramatically more expensive than competitors, forcing customers to reconsider purchases, turning a competitive business on Friday into one facing a “completely different commercial calculation on Monday.” This new economic challenge comes at a time when London’s unemployment rate is already among the highest for large urban centres in Canada.

Graham Henderson likens the current trade conflict to the struggles faced during the 2008 recession and the COVID-19 pandemic. Historically, London has shown resilience; Henderson recalled that the city “sort of went into the recession last and came out first,” a recovery he credits to the city’s “economic diversity” in terms of sectors and export markets.

The concerns extend beyond London. Sarnia Mayor Mike Bradley expressed strong support for the federal government’s response, calling it “excellent” and noting that “most Canadians” support the stance. However, he acknowledged the significant challenges ahead for Southern Ontario.

“Well, right now the tariffs that are coming forward are going to be on plastic. And the auto tariffs are really disturbing because everything that goes into the automobile at some point comes through Sarnia, from the plastic, to the carbon black, to the gasoline itself,” Bradley stated, warning this could “devastate not just our local economy, not just southwestern Ontario, but the entire nation’s economy.” Henderson highlighted that while U.S. tariffs impact about five per cent of Canada’s sales into the U.S. (approximately $20 billion worth of goods), for businesses whose products fall within that five per cent, the problem is much larger.

More than 700 London businesses exported roughly $7.8 billion to the U.S. in 2023, many reliant on that market. Henderson stressed that beyond direct financial costs, an “economic cost that is harder to measure” is uncertainty, making critical business decisions about hiring, investment, and expansion far more difficult when market access can change “dramatically within days.” The consequences ripple outward: If exporters lose orders, their suppliers, transportation companies, and contractors can also suffer, eventually impacting businesses that don’t export at all.

The Chamber of Commerce advocates for continued efforts towards predictable U.S. market access while accelerating trade diversification.

stories.title: ‘It’s ground zero’: Walkerton hosts water safety training for Ontario water operators
stories.summary: Water operators from as far away as Kenora are in Walkerton this week to upgrade their skills through mandatory yearly training.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Water operators from as far away as Kenora are in Walkerton this week to upgrade their skills through mandatory yearly training. “Safe drinking water relies on skilled operators, and not all those skills can happen in a classroom,” said Walkerton Clean Water Centre CEO, Kara Rutherford.

“So, Maintenance Fest provides those practical hands-on skills, using equipment, and real-life scenarios that they can learn from.” While most water system operators came from Southern Ontario to this year’s training, Rick Sandy and Phil Tangie travelled 18 hours to be there from a remote Indigenous nation near the Manitoba border.

“I’m just hoping to learn everything that they provide. And hopefully they can help me in my own community, because I want to provide safe and clean drinking water for my people, where I’m from,” said Sandy, who is a water operator in training with the Anishinaabeg of Naongashiing Nation near Kenora.

It’s not just municipal or Indigenous water operators there, John Bender operates a trailer home park near Durham. He had to get a water operator license 20 years ago and needs yearly training to keep that license. “To be very honest with you, it was very intimidating at first.

Not only because it was new, but because it was regulated, so stringent,” said Bender. “A lot of people got sick here in Walkerton. Some people died because of bad water. Now, in Ontario, we have the safest water in the world.

That’s been brought out at this training a number of times. I learned that it’s not so much about them trying to put me in jail, as it is to educate me, and find a group of people who will help me provide clean water to my tenants.” Bender is one of 68 participants learning about everything to do with water at the 13th year of Maintenance Fest Tuesday and Wednesday.

Since, the Walkerton Clean Water Centre opened in 2010, 125,000 people have been trained in water system safety in the very place where tainted drinking water killed seven people. “To me, it’s ground zero. Well number five, it’s ground zero.

So, whenever I bring operators here, I bring them on a tour to well number five, and we go to the monument, and we talk about the tragedy,” said Tangie, who is the Water Resource Hub Manager, for the Anishinaabeg of Naongashiing Nation near Kenora.

Bender says now that the nerves have dissipated, he’s eager to learn and network with Ontarians in the same boat as him, managing drinking water for others. “Ultimately, I’m in the business of making people happy, and taking care of people,” he said.

stories.title: Former London councillor to stand trial in 2027 on extortion, harassment charges
stories.summary: Mariam Hamou was charged in November with extortion and harassment following an investigation by police in St. Thomas.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content: A trial date has been set for former City of London councillor Mariam Hamou. The former Ward 6 councillor was charged in November with extortion and harassment following an investigation by police in St. Thomas. As required by the Community Safety and Policing Act, the St. Thomas police were called in to investigate the London-based complaint to ensure that was not a conflict of interest, The trial will have two separate dates — Feb. 26 and March 2 of 2027. Shortly after the charges were laid, a ban on publication was placed on any evidence surrounding the charges or the identity of the complainant involved in the matter.

stories.title: Ontario legislature faces calls to return amid trade war. Ford calls it ‘gutter politics’
stories.summary: The trade war between Canada and the United States intensified over the weekend, after talks to secure an agreement fell apart and Prime Minister Mark Carney recalled negotiators.
stories.author: Isaac Callan, Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
Opposition parties at Queen’s Park are calling on Doug Ford to recall the Ontario legislature to debate and pass tariff relief measures, a request the premier dismissed as “gutter politics.”

The trade war between Canada and the United States intensified over the weekend, after talks to secure an agreement fell apart and Prime Minister Mark Carney recalled negotiators to Ottawa.

That meant 50 per cent tariffs came into effect Saturday on billions of dollars in Canadian goods, with United States President Donald Trump threatening more and Canada announcing a “dollar-for-dollar” response.

Premier Ford appeared with steel workers on Monday to reassure businesses he would “spare no expense” protecting workers from the effects of tariffs.

He also said the province is expanding eligibility for its “Protect Ontario” financing program to workers and businesses affected by the new tariffs.

The premier, however, offered few substantive new policy measures and his opponents are arguing politicians should be back in the chamber debating the best response.

“Ontario is looking for its leaders to step up for them,” said Stiles. “To protect their livelihoods and their families. We must stand strong and united from coast to coast to coast.

“It is our duty as elected officials to immediately get to work in the fight against Donald Trump’s inexcusable and dangerous tariffs,” Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles said in a statement.

Her party is advocating for the government to review and cancel any contracts with United States businesses, prohibit data centres with links to U.S. companies and to prioritize made-in-Ontario vehicles for the government’s fleet.

“These times call for a strong and decisive response,” added Stiles. “Doug Ford and his government must take these steps to defend Ontario in the face of Donald Trump’s belligerent attacks on our workers and our economy.”

Asked about the call on Monday, Ford was dismissive.

“I have been in this game a long time. They want to play gutter politics,” Ford said, instead suggesting opposition parties should reach out to him personally.

“Call me up, give me suggestions,” he added. “But make sure when we go back in the legislature, because we will be going back in our time frame, that they actually support things that we put forward.”

Ontario Liberal interim leader John Fraser said the premier wanted to bypass legitimate policy scrutiny.

“There’s something that’s called debate — it’s open, it is public. Doug Ford’s texts aren’t public. His phone and cell phone records aren’t public,” he told reporters Monday.

“This place is here for a reason, and it’s worked for centuries. But now we’re in a situation where we have a premier who believes it doesn’t have a function and it’s not needed. He’s doing the bare minimum.”

Politicians were originally scheduled to be back in the legislature after Labour Day, before the government delayed their return until late October.

— with files from The Canadian Press

Premier Ford appeared with steel workers on Monday to reassure businesses he would “spare no expense” protecting workers from the effects of tariffs.
He also said the province is expanding eligibility for its “Protect Ontario” financing program to workers and businesses affected by the new tariffs.
The premier, however, offered few substantive new policy measures and his opponents are arguing politicians should be back in the chamber debating the best response.
“Ontario is looking for its leaders to step up for them,” said Stiles. “To protect their livelihoods and their families. We must stand strong and united from coast to coast to coast.
“It is our duty as elected officials to immediately get to work in the fight against Donald Trump’s inexcusable and dangerous tariffs,” Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles said in a statement.

Her party is advocating for the government to review and cancel any contracts with United States businesses, prohibit data centres with links to U.S. companies and to prioritize made-in-Ontario vehicles for the government’s fleet.

“These times call for a strong and decisive response,” added Stiles. “Doug Ford and his government must take these steps to defend Ontario in the face of Donald Trump’s belligerent attacks on our workers and our economy.”
Asked about the call on Monday, Ford was dismissive.
“I have been in this game a long time. They want to play gutter politics,” Ford said, instead suggesting opposition parties should reach out to him personally.

“Call me up, give me suggestions,” he added. “But make sure when we go back in the legislature, because we will be going back in our time frame, that they actually support things that we put forward.”
Ontario Liberal interim leader John Fraser said the premier wanted to bypass legitimate policy scrutiny.
“There’s something that’s called debate — it’s open, it is public. Doug Ford’s texts aren’t public. His phone and cell phone records aren’t public,” he told reporters Monday.

“This place is here for a reason, and it’s worked for centuries. But now we’re in a situation where we have a premier who believes it doesn’t have a function and it’s not needed. He’s doing the bare minimum.”
Politicians were originally scheduled to be back in the legislature after Labour Day, before the government delayed their return until late October.

stories.title: London tenant facing homelessness as advocates call for stronger ‘demoviction’ protections
stories.summary: A London tenant facing eviction says he could be homeless within days as tenant advocates call on the city to strengthen protections against what they describe as ‘demovictions.’
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
A London tenant facing eviction says he could be homeless within days as tenant advocates call on the city to strengthen protections against what they describe as ‘demovictions.’ Darcy Barnes, 63, has lived in a unit at 34 Adelaide Street South for about 10 years.

He says he is on disability, as he awaits a double hip surgery. “Homelessness, basically. I’m debilitated,” Barnes said during a tenant rally outside his home Tuesday. “I have osteoarthritis in both hips. Nerve pain in my leg.

And I can’t get my furniture out of the house. And I have nowhere to bring it.” Barnes says his landlord served him a N13 eviction notice last year, saying the unit needed to be vacated for work involving the building. A N13 notice can be used by landlords when a rental unit is needed for demolition, conversion, or extensive repairs or renovations.

Barnes challenged the eviction at the Landlord and Tenant Board but lost his case in July. “Now I don’t have any options with my health and I’m just begging for help basically,” Barnes said. Barnes says he has been in contact with London’s Coordinated Access program and has an intake appointment scheduled for September.

He says he is concerned that appointment will come too late. Tenant advocacy group Acorn London organized Tuesday’s rally and is calling on the City of London to close what it describes as a loophole in the city’s renoviction protections.

“Darcy is the vulnerable tenant that we’ve been talking about for, you know, for the years that we’ve been organizing here,” said Jordan Smith of Acorn London. “Darcy is the example.” London’s Rental Unit Repair Licence bylaw requires landlords seeking to evict tenants for extensive repairs or renovations to meet additional municipal requirements.

However, the city’s rental unit repair licence does not apply to N13 notices issued for demolition or conversion. Those cases are primarily governed by Ontario’s Residential Tenancies Act and the Landlord and Tenant Board.

Acorn says the distinction leaves tenants vulnerable to displacement when a landlord uses a N13 for demolition or conversion. “It leaves him completely stuck,” Smith said. “It leaves him homeless in the next few months, unless one of our councillors steps in and someone, a champion from the city, steps in and puts their money where their mouth is and protects the vulnerable tenants.” Acorn is calling on the city to adopt stronger, enforceable protections against demovictions and to provide immediate housing support for vulnerable tenants facing displacement.

Smith also alleges the work cited in Barnes’ eviction does not match what has happened at the property. “The whole purpose was originally that five units were going to be converted into two, and that’s just not happened,” Smith said.

“In fact, the landlord has gone and rented the units that were vacant.” Those allegations have not been independently verified. CTV News contacted the landlord by phone and email seeking comment on Barnes’ eviction and the allegations raised by Acorn.

He did not respond. The property at 34 Adelaide Street South has previously been the subject of a planning application before the city. In November 2025, London city council approved a zoning amendment for the property that recognized the existing converted dwelling and permitted up to six residential units.

City protections don’t cover demolition N13s. The City of London’s current renoviction rules are intended to provide additional protections for tenants when landlords require vacant possession to carry out extensive repairs or renovations.

However, the municipal Rental Unit Repair Licence does not apply when a N13 is issued for demolition or conversion. The city has previously considered whether to expand its renoviction protections to cover those situations.

Council has so far declined to make that change, while broader tenant protections related to demolition and redevelopment could be considered as part of future municipal policy work. For Barnes, the debate over how London’s rental housing rules should change is now immediate.

He says his health makes finding another home particularly difficult and he fears he will have nowhere to go when he is required to leave.

stories.title: Blue Jays’ Dylan Cease launches capsule collection at AGO
stories.summary: Toronto Blue Jays' Dylan Cease has teamed up with the Art Gallery of Ontario to show off one of his paintings and release a limited-edition merch line.
stories.author: Megan King
stories.content:
Sports fans and art lovers collided at the Art Gallery of Ontario (AGO) Tuesday as a limited-edition capsule collection was revealed.

It includes prints, postcards, clothing and totes featuring the painting “Eve of Toronto” created by Blue Jays’ pitcher Dylan Cease.

“I get to enjoy doing the painting, I get to show it off and let everyone see it and then we also get to make money and have it all go to good causes,” said Cease. “It’s all a lot of positivity stacked on each other.”

Proceeds from the AGO x Cease collection will support the art gallery’s charitable mission: enriching lives through art and learning.

AGO chief brand and business officer Ros Lawler also hopes it will spark people’s interest in the arts.

“Dylan was saying earlier how he first got interested in art was because he had a very stressful season of baseball, it’s pretty intense, and he went to an art museum,” said Lawler.

“He found he was really relaxed and inspired and that’s kind of what got him involved. I think we can all use a bit of that in our daily lives.”

“Eve of Toronto” first debuted in Blue Jays’ General Manager John Schneiders’ office.

The piece is described as a love letter to the city.

“It’s almost like my calling card that I get to shoutout where I’m at and what I’m playing and fighting for,” Cease said. “So, it just feels right.”

Through the AGO, he is now sharing that feeling with the many fans who showed up.

“It’s so rare to have this level of artistry while you’re one of the best athletes in your game,” said baseball and art fan Lesley Mak. “It’s a double whammy that I can’t even believe is possible in one person, but he’s that guy.”

Cease said he uses the creative outlet to freely experiment in a way that he can’t during baseball.

This collaboration giving him a chance to express himself to the city.

“It feels really good,” Cease said. “It’s just fun to, honestly, be a part of the community.”
